title: Free Financial Literacy Activities for Primary School
metaDescription: Six free, low-prep group activities for teaching primary school children about money, using paper, pictures and imaginary budgets only.

sections.heading: What makes these activities different
paragraphs: Everything here runs on paper, pictures and imaginary money — no accounts, no app, no printing budget beyond a few price cards. That makes these activities genuinely free and genuinely low-prep: most can be set up in the time it takes to write six prices on cards and cut them out.

They're also specifically designed for pairs, small groups or a whole class working together, which is a different angle from an individual or digital money game. If you're after single-player or screen-based games instead, our guide to money games for kids covers that separately — this guide is about shared, talk-it-through activities where pupils reason out loud and justify choices to each other, not ones a child plays alone.

Each activity below gives one clear objective, works with a fictional budget, and ends with a question that reveals whether pupils actually understood the reasoning, not just whether they filled in an answer.

sections.heading: 1. The £10 shopping challenge
paragraphs: Give pairs of pupils a fictional £10 budget (a UK-style example in pounds — adjust the currency for your own classroom) and picture cards showing a sandwich (£3), fruit (£2), a drink (£2) and a toy (£6). Ask them to plan a basket and explain out loud what they chose to leave out and why.

Once most pairs have a basket, change one price — raise the sandwich to £4, for instance — and ask them to revise their plan. The objective is reasoning within a changing budget, not landing on one single "correct" basket, so resist the urge to reveal an ideal answer at the end.

sections.heading: 2. Needs and wants sorting
paragraphs: Provide picture cards for food, shelter, a bus ticket, a game and a birthday gift, and ask pupils to sort them into needs and wants. The useful follow-up question is why an item might move category depending on context: a bus ticket may be essential for one family's daily routine and entirely optional for another.

This is a good activity for surfacing different family situations without putting any one pupil's circumstances on display — keep all the examples on the cards fictional, and avoid asking pupils to compare the cards to their own family's real purchases.

sections.heading: 3. The saving timeline
paragraphs: Draw four weekly boxes on the board or on paper. A fictional character wants an £8 item and saves £2 a week. Pupils add coins, tally marks or stickers to each box as the weeks pass, then answer: how many weeks until the character can afford it?

Add a complication once the basic version works: what happens if the price rises to £10 partway through? For pupils who find handwriting difficult, swap in movable counters or digital tokens on a tablet rather than asking them to draw in each box.

sections.heading: 4. Design a tiny business
paragraphs: Teams choose a pretend product, estimate what it costs to make, and set a selling price. Give each team three fictional customer requests and ask how they'd respond to each one.

Use this activity to introduce one specific distinction clearly: revenue is the money a business receives, while profit is what's left once costs are subtracted — the two get conflated constantly, including by adults, so it's worth stating the difference explicitly rather than assuming it's obvious. Avoid implying that every business idea in the room will succeed; a team whose costs outweigh their price is learning something just as useful as a team that turns a profit.

sections.heading: 5. Spot the suspicious message
paragraphs: Show pupils a fictional message asking someone to click an urgent payment link. Ask them to circle pressure words ("now," "urgent," "final warning"), identify what evidence is missing, and practise the response of asking a trusted adult before acting on anything like it.

Keep this entirely hypothetical: use invented names, invented amounts, and never a real account number, real link or real company name. The skill being practised is the pause-and-check habit, not identification of any specific real-world scam.

sections.heading: 6. Reflection and assessment: the one question that matters
paragraphs: Finish any of the activities above with a single question: "What did you choose, and why?" Accept spoken, written, picture or AAC (augmentative and alternative communication) responses equally — the format doesn't matter, the reasoning does.

A successful activity is one where the answer reveals the pupil's thinking, not one where every pupil arrives at the same answer. It's usually more valuable to reuse an activity with new prices the following week than to pile a new, more complex activity on top before the first one has settled in.

sections.heading: Worked example: planning a fictional picnic on a budget
paragraphs: A class plans a fictional picnic for four people on an £18 budget (again, a UK-style figure to adjust as needed). Each group receives price cards for sandwiches, fruit, water and one decorative extra, such as bunting or napkins.

Ask each group to explain how they included food and drink before any optional extras, then introduce a change — one price rises — and ask them to adapt their plan. This mirrors the shopping challenge above but at a slightly larger scale, which works well as a second or third session once pupils are comfortable with the basic format.

sections.heading: A simple four-step lesson plan
paragraphs: However you combine the activities above, this structure keeps a session focused:
list: Choose one objective for the session, such as calculating change or justifying priorities — not several at once.
Give every group the same fictional price list and accessible visual cards.
Offer counters, calculators or AAC as appropriate to the specific learning objective, not as an afterthought.
Finish with an exit ticket showing one new price, and ask each pupil for a revised plan.

sections.heading: How to check pupils actually understood
paragraphs: The most reliable check is whether a pupil can apply the same rule to different items, not whether they can repeat the exact example you used in class. After any activity, swap in two or three new items at new prices and ask pupils to explain their choice again using words, pictures or symbols.

A pupil who can only solve the version with the exact numbers you demonstrated has memorised an answer, not learned the reasoning behind it — that's a useful distinction to hold onto when deciding whether to move on to a harder version or repeat the same one with new numbers.

sections.heading: Making these activities accessible for every pupil
paragraphs: Every activity above can be run with the whole class, but not every pupil will show understanding the same way, and these are worth planning for rather than fixing on the day. For a pupil with SEND (special educational needs and disabilities), reduce visual and auditory clutter on the cards themselves — one item per card, high contrast, no competing background pattern — and give noticeably more processing time before expecting a response in a group setting.

For a pupil who uses AAC, build their existing vocabulary board into the activity directly: core words like "more," "less," "same" and "choose" cover most of what these activities ask for, so there's rarely a need for a bespoke vocabulary set. A pupil can also demonstrate the full reasoning non-verbally — sorting physical cards into piles, pointing to a sequence of pictures, or using eye gaze with a partner reading out the options — and any of these count as a complete answer, not a partial one.

sections.heading: A common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: Don't assume every pupil already knows local coins, has spending money at home, or has shopped unsupervised — any of these assumptions can leave some pupils guessing at vocabulary rather than reasoning about money. Teach the relevant vocabulary (price, budget, change, cost) explicitly before testing it in an activity, rather than assuming it arrives already in place.

sections.heading: Try this next
paragraphs: Pick one activity from this guide and run it this week with a different fictional example than the ones shown here. Ask pupils to explain a choice, show it with pictures, or communicate it using their preferred method, and plan to reuse the same activity with new numbers before adding a new one.

sections.heading: Editorial references
paragraphs: Guidance from the Money and Pensions Service on children and young people's financial education supports building financial understanding through concrete, repeated, real-world-style decisions rather than one-off lessons: https://maps.org.uk/en/our-work/children-and-young-people

The Education Endowment Foundation's guidance on metacognition and self-regulation supports asking pupils to explain their reasoning aloud as a way of building transferable thinking skills, which is the basis for the "what did you choose, and why" question used throughout this guide: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/metacognition-and-self-regulation

faqs.question: How long should each activity take?
faqs.answer: Start with a short session of around ten to fifteen minutes, then adapt to the group's attention span and access needs. That's a practical starting point rather than a research-established optimum, so a shorter or longer session is perfectly fine.

faqs.question: What if a pupil gives an unexpected answer?
faqs.answer: Ask for the reasoning behind it, check whether the instructions were understood, and offer another example before assuming the answer was simply wrong. Avoid treating speed or confident talking as a proxy for genuine financial understanding.

faqs.question: Do I need any materials or a budget for these?
faqs.answer: No. Every activity here uses paper, hand-drawn or printed picture cards, and imaginary money — there's no cost beyond a few minutes of preparation, and nothing here requires an app, an account or real money of any kind.
